reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Vesicoureteric reflux is the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder up the ureter toward the kidney, predisposing to recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring, mainly in children

Primary VUR results from a congenitally short or abnormal submucosal ureteric tunnel with an incompetent vesicoureteric junction, whereas secondary VUR arises from raised bladder pressure due to obstruction or a neurogenic or dysfunctional bladder
It commonly presents with febrile urinary tract infections in infancy or childhood, or is detected during investigation of antenatal hydronephrosis
Severity is graded I to V by the voiding cystourethrogram appearance, from reflux confined to a non-dilated ureter up to gross dilatation and tortuosity with a severely dilated collecting system
The principal concern is reflux nephropathy: renal scarring from recurrent infection combined with reflux, which can lead to hypertension, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease
Voiding cystourethrography is the standard test to confirm and grade reflux, while DMSA scintigraphy detects renal scarring and pyelonephritis

Management principles emphasise prevention and prompt treatment of infection, attention to bladder and bowel dysfunction, and continuous antibiotic prophylaxis in selected children, since many low-grade cases resolve spontaneously with growth
Surgical or endoscopic correction (ureteric reimplantation or subureteric injection) is reserved for high-grade, persistent, or breakthrough-infection cases
reference.pathophysiology: Vesicoureteric reflux occurs when the valve-like mechanism of the vesicoureteric junction fails, allowing urine to reflux from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis. Normally an adequate length of submucosal ureter within the bladder wall is compressed during bladder filling and voiding, preventing reflux; in primary VUR this tunnel is congenitally short or laterally placed. Secondary VUR develops when high intravesical pressures from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic/dysfunctional voiding overcome the junction. Reflux of infected urine and elevated pressures transmitted to the kidney cause pyelonephritis and scarring (reflux nephropathy), which underlies later hypertension and renal impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent urinary tract infection without reflux
Obstructive uropathy (posterior urethral valves, PUJ obstruction)
Duplex collecting system with ectopic ureter or ureterocele
additionalInvestigations: Voiding (micturating) cystourethrography to confirm and grade reflux
DMSA renal scintigraphy to detect scarring and acute pyelonephritis
Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess for dilatation and anatomy
Urinalysis and culture during febrile illness
Assessment of renal function and blood pressure
Evaluation of bladder and bowel function (uroflowmetry, voiding diary) in older children
redFlags: Febrile urinary tract infection with an obstructed or refluxing system risking urosepsis, a urological emergency requiring prompt drainage and antibiotics
Progressive renal scarring or reduced differential renal function
New or worsening hypertension or proteinuria indicating reflux nephropathy
High-grade reflux with breakthrough infections despite prophylaxis
Bilateral high-grade reflux with impaired renal function
reference.prognosis: Many children with low-grade primary reflux resolve spontaneously as they grow and do well with infection prevention; high-grade reflux, recurrent pyelonephritis, and established scarring carry a greater risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, making surveillance important.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate recurrent febrile UTIs in a child for underlying reflux
Overlooking bladder and bowel dysfunction, which perpetuates reflux and infection
Missing secondary reflux from obstruction such as posterior urethral valves
Neglecting long-term monitoring of blood pressure and renal function in children with scarring
Delaying treatment of a febrile infection in an obstructed, refluxing system
management: Optimise bladder and bowel function first, treating constipation and dysfunctional voiding with timed voiding and a bowel regimen to reduce infection and aid resolution
Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis for infants and children with high-grade reflux or recurrent febrile urinary tract infections
Conservative observation with infection prevention for low-grade primary reflux, anticipating spontaneous resolution with growth
Treat febrile urinary tract infections promptly with culture-directed antibiotics to minimise reflux nephropathy
Endoscopic subureteric injection or open ureteric reimplantation for persistent high-grade reflux or breakthrough pyelonephritis despite prophylaxis
Regular surveillance with renal tract ultrasound, DMSA scanning for scarring, blood pressure and renal function assessment
Involve paediatric urology and nephrology, escalating if hypertension, proteinuria or chronic kidney disease develop
